speechtext: I have received the information from the Postmaster General. I am sorry I have not got it with me, I will give it to my hon. friend to-morrow.

For the development of the live stock, dairying and fruit industries, the improvement of seeds, and the promotion of the sale of fool and other agricultural products ; employees paid from this sum not to be subject to the Civil Service Act, $220,000.
iMr. FISHER. I may say that this is a regular vote taken every year for the Agriculture Department. It has heretofore been administered under the supervision of the Commissioner of Agriculture and Dairying, Prof. Robertson. Perhaps I ought at once to explain that during this fiscal year Prof. Robertson has banded in his resignation and has severed his connection with the department. I need hardy dwell upon the regret which I personally feel at the loss of so eminent, and successful, ami painstaking a public servant. My only relief at his loss Is the knowledge that although he has left the service of the government. Professor Robertson still serves the agricultural interests of Canada, having taken a position in the control and management of a great agricultural station or college which is to be established on the island of Montreal through the beneficence of Sir William McDonald. I bad a conversation wltb Professor Robertson not long before this step was taken, and bad the advantage of discussing with him the future arrangements for carrying on this work. I think it is not necessary to appoint anybody to take his place. Under Professor Robertson the work for which this money has been voted was divided into three divisions, each one having an efficient officer at its head. I think that each of these officers is well qualified to take charge of the divisions with which they were specially charged, when they reported directly to the deputy minister and through him to me. I have now organized this work on that basis, and it is moving very satisfactorily. I think that no harm to the public service will come from it. While I regret extremely the loss of Professor Robertson's services to the country and to myself, I feel satisfied that the departmental work will go on very satisfactorily under the charge of Mr. Ruddick, Commissioner of Dairying, Mr. Hodgson, Commissioner of Live Stock, and Mr. Clark, Commissioner for seeds and seed growing, each of these being directly responsible through the deputy minister to myself, in the same way that Professor Robertson was before. The vote is still the same vote, but it is being divided amongst these three divisions.

Why do you not
take three votes and give us the sum for each ?

I do not think there is any necessity for dividing the vote. I was going to give a short outline of the way this money will be spent. The dairy commissioner has about $130,000, the commissioner for seeds about $35,000 and the live stock commissioner about $50,000. This leaves about $5,000

not devoted to any one of these great divisions, but retained for any agricultural work that may arise during the year for which no other provision may have been made. I would instance some investigations in regard to the growth of tobacco which have been carried on in recent years under Professor Robertson, but not under any one of these officers n*io had charge of a division under Professor Robertson. With regard to these three great divisions, 1 may explain that the dairy commissioner has charge, not only of the dairy work-the cool curing rooms for flheese which we have been running for two or three years, the creameries in the Northwest which we have been running for many' years, and the cold storage work of the country generally-but also what is called the extension of markets for Canadian food products. This latter includes the inspection and management in regard to the shipping of our different products, the question of prices, and also the work of our officials in England, who watch the arrival of our food products in. that great market. The administration of the Fruit Inspection Act and the Fruit Marks Act also come under this division, which has to do with what we call the commercial work -the management of the transportation and handling of our food products which this great branch, under Professor Robertson, has always dealt with. The live stock commissioner's branch carries on the work we do on behalf of the live stock interests of Canada, the keeping of the records which I explained to the House a little while ago, the sales of live stock throughout the country ; the work we do in connection with farmers' institutes ; the work we do in connection with the exhibitions, trying to bring them to uniform lines and helping them by supplying judges ; and also the work we do in connection with the interprovincial trade in live stock which has arisen of late years, and which has called for a good deal of supervision and assistance in the way of spreading information among the people as to the supplies of live stock that may be had from different parts of the country. The seed division will cover two main items. The first is the work we are doing to promote the use of (better and cleaner seed. And now that the Seed Control Act has passed this House, and, I hope, will pass the Senate soon and will become law, the second item will be the administration of that Act. In connection with this branch we are encouraging and helping the formation of seed-growers' associations all over the country, by means of which we hope to get men interested in growing better seed for use on our farms. I regret to say that many of our farmers are careless with regard" to the quality of seed they use. There is immense room for improvement, not only in the varieties of seed which ought to be used, but also in the use of good, well-matured seed, which will be sure to germinate and seed which is clean and free from weeds. When I say that our farmers have been careless in this respect, of course, a large number .of our best farmers are very particular on this point, and have been doing good work both in the seed they have produced and in the choice of seed for use on their farms. Still, there is an immense number of our farmers who do not seem to understand the importance of watching closely the quality of the seed they use. The consequence has been, in many instances, that the crops have deteriorated, not only in quality, but in quantity.
This, in general outline, is the work covered by these divisions. I have a staff of, I believe, efficient and, 1 know, enthusiastic and energetic officers to deal with these matters, and I have proof from all parts of the country of the good work that is being done. I believe that the money spent in years past has been productive of great good, and I trust that in future increasing advantage will accrue to (the Dominion through this branch of the public service.

It seems to me objectionable that the minister should have so large a vote to devote to any purpose he chooses within these very wide lines. The vote should be divided-so much for dairies, so much for live stock, so much for seed and so much for markets. When the Auditor General comes to look over this expenditure he will find no means of checking it, so long as it has been spent for any one of the things here mentioned. The minister may stand by what he says to-night or he may change-there is nothing to prevent him. If he knows what we want for each of these branches, I do not see why this vote should not be divided. If that is done, the minister can be held to account by the Auditor General. Perhaps that is the very thing the hon. gentleman does not want. I find that the vote for immigration is included in about three items, covering about $700,000 or $800,000. I think it is about time we had these estimates divided more carefully, so that we may know what we are voting, and so that the" ministers may be held strictly to account for the expenditure of these large sums.
(Mr. FISHER. We have not found any difficulty with regard to that in the past. I have always been ready to give full information on the subject. Occasionally, of course, one particular line of work costs a little more than is expected, but, under such a vote as this, it can be done, and so the public work can go on effectively.
.Mr. URIAH WTUSON, What objection has the minister to dividing this up in the manner I suggest ?

I may tell the hon. member frankly that my chief objection is that if you meet an unforeseen difficulty, involving

a change in the estimates, it generally requires more discussion and explanation in the House. This vote is not changed from what it has been. Tile only difference is that the head has been removed and the whole has been brought under the deputy minister. Formerly it was under the control of Professor Robertson. That is the only change. Otherwise, when this was voted for Professor Robertson's branch last year it was voted just in the same way as I am asking to have it voted now.	'
When Mr. Robertson was head he had control of the three departments for which the minister is now to have three gentlemen.
As a matter of fact Professor Robertson had five or six departments un'der him and they were just as separate as they are to-day.
I beg pardon, Mr. Minister. Professor Robertson had control of the three departments you have taken here, and he was responsible to the deputy minister for the conduct of these three departments.

No, excuse me, Professor Robertson was independent of the deputy minister.
is a good deal of fraud in connection with ; this matter, and when the minister tells this House and the country that the farmers do not know enough to select the seed to sow on their farms I want to tell him he was brought up in a section of country that is not very intelligent, and he must not speak from that section of the country for the farmers of Ontario. The farmers of Ontario know how to select their seed as well as any official he has in his department and it would not take them half so long to put it in concise language so that a man of ordinary intelligence would know what it meant.

I do not think the minister has given a very good reason why this vote is a lump sum. The fact that it has been done before to my mind is no reason why it should be continued unless it is the best way. If the minister has an outline in his mind of what he wants for each of these departments, each of these items, I think that is the way to put it in the estimates, and then he would not spend any more than the amount specified on any particular service without coming back to the House for another vote. I think it would be better if the minister cannot do it this year to consider it another year.
He was responsible to you.
Yes, he was responsible to me. Now the deputy minister is responsible.

If you want to do all the talking let us know it. The minister is a good deal like his officials ; unless he has a great amount of verbiage to give us a little information, he does not think he is doing anything.
I will not do it any more.

We want you to do more, but it is better for the minister to answer the question and sit down and not do all the talking before the committee. I was right, Professor Robertson was responsible to you if not to the deputy and there "'as one man who controlled this money and now you have three controlling it responsible to the deputy and the deputy is responsible to you, so we do not know where it is going and you may spend money on departments, for which we do not vote it at all. We leave it just to your sweet will to spend this money where you see fit. We hear a good deal about the efficient work of these gentlemen but when I wanted to get from the minister himself in the committee the name of one of these gentlemen in order to get some seed, I could not get the information, but I found out from a circular sent to me that there is one man in East Northumberland whom I know very well who would not be able to supply half a dozen farmers Vi ith ten bushels apiece. I do not suppose he had any grain of the kind. I think there Mr. FISHER.
It is well worth considering.

I think what the hon. member (Mr. Uriah Wilson) has said is very true. The same argument that the minister uses might very well be used for simply saying we should vote to the Minister of Agriculture for such purposes as he has mentioned the sum of 1525,600 in the belief that he will use it properly, in the proper proportion for each item. An estimate is for two things. It Is in the first place to define to parliament what you want a certain amount of money for, and in the second place it is to give the auditing officer a chance to check according to the law and to see that no amount shall be expended except for the specific purpose for which it is voted. You put $220,000 in a lump sum and say : This is for the development of live stock, dairying, the fruit industry, improving the state of trade and agricultural products. You lump them together and it is absolutely at the will of the minister first and of Council afterwards. You could use that sum as you choose. The essence of every proper estimate is definiteness. You ought to know about what you are likely to spend on live stock, dairying and each of these other branches. There are at least five or six different specific objects there, and each vote should be divided so that it would be definite and clear ; as it is it is a lump sum. Something of this kind to a certain extent may have always been done, but 1 know when I had to do with estimates my purpose was to get them definitely stated. We happened this year to be ques-
JTTT^e 5. 1905
tioning the Minister of Militia with reference to a lump vote. It appeared innocuous and it seemed to show that it was for a certain purpose that when we came to question him we found that he was undertaking three or four different works with it, in different parts of the country and in different provinces, and unless the question had happened to come up at that time, the city of Fredericton for instance would never have known that in that vote was included a sum to he spent for certain military works there. In proportion as you gather these different items and put them in a general vote, you do away with the definiteness of your estimates and you do away with the guard that the Auditor General has over them. The minister does more than that, he lays up trouble for himself. Influential supporters may come to him and say : Here is a project that we want you to carry out in the line of one of these things. You say :	I
was not proposing to spend this much." But they will reply : But your vote does not tie you, it allows you to do as you please ; what we want you to do is to spend a lot of this money say for this fruit enterprise. The minister lays himself open, at least he takes away from himself this guard that he has definitely told parliament what he would use this money for, and he must keep his pledge to parliament. I call the attention of the minister to that and I would particularly call the attention of the Minister of Finance to it if he were here. I agree with what my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson) has said and I think we must certainly insist on having these estimates divided. I am not going to insist as my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson) did not insist that it should be done for this year, but after this I am going to make a plea with the Finance Minister who supervises these estimates that he shall ask each minister to definitely show each vote. Of course you cannot go into every detail ; you must have some omnibus votes but, omnibus votes should be few and small.

The general principle which my hon. friend has enunciated is undoubtedly correct. This vote is a large one to-day. It has been growing steadily from the needs of the country. I can remember this vote long before I came into office as a vote for some of the purposes which are included in it now. These are all cognate objects. They are not different. They are very largely interlaced ; that is to say some of the men in connection with this vote attend to part of the work and attend also to other parts of the work, and it is a difficult thing to exactly divide the proportions of their time which may be applied to one piece of the work or applied to another piece of the work. I am trying to do that to a certain extent. I find that where it is possible to avoid that it is better because an officer who is shifted about from one work to another, I find, is
not very likely to be effective. I therefore have been trying to get the staff divided, and when the time comes that I can divide this work I think it will be well to do as my hon. friend has suggested, but at the present time I would like to ascertain by experience how much each of these piece's of work will require.
You will have this year to try it in.
Yes, but it is only three months since Professor Robertson resigned and I have only begun the reorganization,
You will have a year from the 1st of July.

1 will have a year after July in which to test the success of it after I have reorganized it if I get this little vote. I know my hon. friend is quite willing to have this little vote go through this year and I appreciate that courtesy on his part. I will say quite frankly to my hon. frieud that when I ask for that item for the succeeding year I will have such information as will enable me to divide it in a way that will meet the wishes of the House. I do not take exception to the criticism that is made. I think that in regard to a vote of these proportions the criticism is to some extent justified. When this vote was originally taken it was a comparatively small affair, but it has increased from year to year and I think that when it has reached its present proportion what my hon. friend from North Toronto Mr. Foster) says has a good deal of justification. When it was a very much smaller vote it was not so necessary to discuss the features of it. But, I will carefully look into the question and see if, in another year, I cannot meet my hon. friend's desires so that the House can thoroughly understand what the money is intended for. I need not say that I have no intention of hiding from the House what the money is intended for.
To promote dairying interests for advance of milk and cream, to be recouped out of the process of sales of such butter and cheese, to be placed to the credit of the consolidated revenue fund, $40,000.
What was done with that vote last year and what was recouped?

We run certain creameries in the Northwest Territories and in making sales of the produce of these creameries we advance a portion of the money at once to the patrons; then, when we come to complete the sales aud get tbe money from the purchasers, we reimburse the treasury and the result is that at the end of the year this money is all back. But, in the meantime we have to have it in the bank to draw upon. A portion of it, I do not know how much, is drawn upon. Some

years only a little is drawn sometimes it runs -pretty close to the amount.
You are out the interest. I suppose ?

We do not charge interest. My officials tell me that it would hardly be safe to undertake the work unless we had available this $40,000. Last year we had something over $100,000 worth of butter. We had to sell that and to handle it and for that purpose my officers think that about $40,000 is needed.
Was there any loss in the transaction to the government last year?

There was no loss except the interest. There was never any loss. The money advanced comes back and more too. We only advance a proportion of the price. We advance 10 cents a pound and the price of butter is 20 cents a pound and over.

What was the nature of the transaction last year and what is the policy? Are you continuing to do the same thing year after year in the same locality, or are you trying to put an industry on its legs, and then go to another locality and try to do the same thing ?

I do not think my hon, friend understands the situation. A good many years ago-I think the very first year after I came into office-representations were made to me that certain creameries had been started in the Northwest Territories chiefly in the Alberta district as private creameries and had failed and that the plant and buildings were there lying useless. I was asked to see if I could not do something to restart the industry there.
I had Professor Robertson look into the matter very closely and we came to the conclusion that there was an opportunity for the establishment of a successful creamery industry in the Northwest Territories. To do that we undertook to advance some money to some of the creameries so as to put them on their feet and to manage and run them. It is in the management and running of them that this money is required. It is only those creameries in the Northwest Territories that are built; we have not for a number of years back started many new ones. I think there was one new one started last year, but most of the older ones have paid up their advances and are paying their way. We are still managing them. I have been informing the people that they must look forward in the near future to our handing over the management to the patrons. We have been begged from year to year not to do it and it has been represented that the management by government officials has been on the whole satisfactory and more successful, especially in the maraeting of their products than Mr. FISHER.
private management. Up to the present time I have not discontinued this system, but I did instruct my officers who went there last winter to say that as a considerable number of the people there were now paying their way and doing well enough to assume the management themselves, I must Insist on their taking over the management and so reducing the resposibility of the government.

I must say that the sting is in the tail and that the last sentence or two of the hon. minister came down to really what I did want to know. With all due deference to the hon. minister I did know exactly how this was being carried on. Is the government going into this in perpetuity ?
No.

Are you always going to take charge of these creameries and run them, or are you just taking hold of them and putting them on a basis where they will be established and self-sustaining, and then say to the people: Here, we have shown you how to do it, we have brought you through a certain amount of instructive practice and now you must take this over yourselves ?
That is the intention.

The government surely does not intend to be running these factories in this way ? How many of these are you running in the Northwest ?
Mr. FISHER, Sixteen, I think.

After you run these for two or three years you must have half of them or more on a fairly good basis, and the people then will know their benefits-. If you are going to go into a certain amount of that business for educative purposes, I presume you will try and get say eight of them on to a self-management basis, and then you could take up another eight districts if you wish. It is the people's work and not the work of government, and -there can be no excuse for the government doing it except that by its-' educative influence it may point out the right way of making and marketing the article.

I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Foster). He has outlined the policy I wish to pursue, but every time I try to drop a creamery the people protest and beg us to continue, and so long as we are doing some of them it is not very much extra expense to do the whole of them. With the influx of settlers there will be other parts of the Northwest Territories which will want to start these creameries soon, but where wheat growing is successful, they do not care to go into dairying.

I understand the minister to state that for this $40,000 of advances

the country was recouped by the sale of the butter, and that that money was paid to the credit of the consolidated fund.

Oh, no. The patrons send their cream to the factory and the butter is sent to a central warehouse at Calgary and disposed of on the open market. The accounts are made up for each individual patron of the factory and when the monthly statements are prepared, frequently the butter is not sold or perhaps only part of it is sold. In the meantime we pay to every patron what is .equal to 10 cents on every pound of butter which his milk has produced. Then when the sales are consummated and the money received for the butter, we pay him the balance according to the price received. None of it is paid to the consolidated fund ; it is a separate fund for each creamery and nothing comes back to the country except perhaps a charge for making.
The item says 1 the proceeds of sales of such butter and cheese to be placed to the credit of the consolidated fund.'
Quite so, but it is not put into the ordinary revenue of the country. It is' a special account for each cream. ery.
Then the country gets no money return whatever for the expenditure of this $40,000 ?

The $40,0o0 is not spent. At the end of the fiscal year the $40,000 is intact ; we simply pay 10 cents on account, for every pound of butter and we pay it out of this vote.
Mr. FOSTER, What profit do you make ?
We do not make a profit. When the price of the butter is received by our officer he retains' 10 cents for every pound and pays it back to this vote.
In what account will the payment back to the country be found ?

The payments out of this vote and the re-imbursements are all submitted to the Auditor General by a special accountant in my department who has charge of this work ; it includes an immense amount of detail as an account for each patron is. kept.

The item states, that this money is placed to the credit of the consolidated revenue fund. Where can I find in the Consolidated Revenue Fund account a statement of the recouping of this money, or any portion of it?
I am afraid I cannot tell the hon. gentleman exactly.

I have the Consolidated Revenue account here, and the only item I can see which would refer even in a distant
way to this item is : ' Department of Agriculture ; special account, $4,855.'

I know in general terms hew it is done, but I am afraid I cannot say as to how it appears in the Public Accounts. Perhaps I have not made myself clear to my hon. friend, who probably is not familiar with the way in which these cooperative factories are worked. Each patron sends his milk or cream to the factory and gets credit for so much butter fat ; and when the total amount of the butter fat is made up into butter and the butter is sold, the money received for it is distributed to the patrons in proportion to what they have sent to the factory. Before that final distribution occurs, however, my officer pays tto each patron 10 cents per pound on account out of this fund. When the final sale of the butter takes place and the money is received by my officer, he pays back into this fund the 10 cents which he had advanced out of it to each patron, and then pays the balance to the pahrons in addition.

What we still do not understand is where the country gets recouped.
I understood the minister to state that the $40,000 was merely handled, and the country got it all back. If that is the case, there ought to be some entry of that repayment in the public accounts ; but I can find no such entry.

I cannot explain that, but I think it is due to the fact that at the beginning of the year a credit is given by the Auditor General to the Department of Agriculture ; my officers from time to time use what they want of it, and replace it before the end of the year. Consequently, it would not appear as impaired in any way ; and, in consequence of that, I suppose it does not appear in the public accounts at all.
I think this is a fair item to stand until the minister can give us that information. Is there an officer in every factory ; and if so, is he paid by the patrons ?
We pay the officers and we charge the patrons so much for making the butter.

How much money was actually paid out last year to these patrons at the rate of 10 cents a pound ?
Mr. FISHER, I have not that information at my hand. I can find out immediately the number of pounds of butter that was made, which would show how much was paid out. Of course, my hon. friend will understand that this $40,000 might be used three or four times over during the season as needed. We pay out the 10 cents when the butter is made in the creamery. We might sell that butter in a week and get the money ail back, or we might not sell it for two or three months, and consequently

be unable to reimburse the fund for that length of time. It is practically a deposit to be used as working capital, and to be recouped when the money comes in.
iM$r. FOSTER. The miiniisiter has not answered clearly the question of the hou. member for St. John. What he wants to know is where that money comes back to the treasury. We can easily understand how it goes out ; but my hon. friend from St. John says that within the covers of the book he cannot find more than $4,000 that has come back. That question has not been answered by the minister. I think we shall have to have this item stand until that can be made clear, and also because two or three of our members who are not here want to say something about these features.
I have no objection to let it stand.
The minister might tell us how much a pound he gets for making the butter, and whether the account comes out even or shows any profit ?
We get 4 cents a pound. In the large creameries that more than covers the cost, while in the small creameries it does not cover the cost.
How do you even up the accounts ?

Where there is any money over we give it to the creamery where it is made ; and where there is a deficit we pay that ourselves. We do not charge the good creameries with the losses of the poor ones.
Item allowed to stand.

speechtext: This is the usual vote for the Senate. It shows an increase of $1,000, of which I am sorry to say I cannot give any explanation. They want that much more to carry on their business.
I am quite sure the House of Commons would never abnegate its right to have an explanation of this increase. We cannot vote money here without knowing what it is for.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Reforming the Senate out of existence?
Reforming it even out of existence; and especially one thing was going to be done, there was going to be no old
Women ?

Women, yes, or defeated candidates, men of an age so advanced that it is difficult for them to get around. Will the right hon. gentleman now tell us exactly tlie age of the last gift made by himself to the Senate ?

Books for the general library, including binding, &c., $13,000.
Has the government considered the need of enlarging the library building?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, the attention of the government has been brought to the necessity of providing additional space for the increasing number of volumes. A plan has been suggested to the government, but we have come to no conclusion. If my hon. friend has views upon the subject, I would be glad to hear them, because the government will approach the subject with an absolutely open mind.

The subject has been brought to my notice by reason of my membership of a committee of the House of Commons. I have been told that another plan has been prepared, but the session is so far advanced that unless the government has finally come to a conclusion, it will be a long time before anything is done. More space is needed. I understand that nearly half the books of the library are hidden, or are in some place where they cannot be seen.
Who has the selection of the new books for the library?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, the Library Committee gives sometimes directions to the librarians, but when no directions are given to the librarians they use their own judgment. But so far as I know, the committee have no control over the librarians regarding the purchase of books, these gentlemen are absolutely their own masters. The committee has never suggested to the librarians how they should employ the money. I think my hon. friend is a member of the Library Committee

I am a member. It meets once, and nothing is done; that is a preliminary meeting to make arrangements for a second meeting. It meets the second time, and a report is read, and then we adjourn. We may have another meeting before the session closes. Sometimes I think there is a lack in the library of up-to-date books. I do not know whether other members have noticed it or not in their requirements for reading, but I have wondered whether the committee had advisory duties in connection with the purchase of new books.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sure that depends altogether on the librarians. There was a time when I was a more faithful attendant of that committee than I have been of late years, and my experience was something like that of my hon. friend, that a meeting was more of a social gathering than anything else. Sometimes we had a general conversation, and a suggestion was made that we should get such and such a book; but nothing was ever done, nothing is done now, the librarians absolutely use their own judgment in the purchase of the books. .

There is another thing, and that is the failure on the part of many who take out books to return them. I do not know how it can be overcome, unless it be done by the passage of resolutions requiring parties to return books taken from the parliamentary library. The librarians are really the servants of parliament, parliament is composed of members, and if there is any collision between the parliamentary librarian and a member, the librarian generally gets the worst of it. At least all he can do is courteously to ask for the books to be returned, but if the member simply does not answer that request. the books are not returned. I think the Prime Minister himself would be surprised if he knew just how many books are absent from the library because, under circumstances that we usually forget, they are not returned. But that is not the purpose for which the library was instituted, it was to keep books in the library itself, in order to afford the advantages both of
quick reading and of circulation. I was wondering whether anything could be done to facilitate the gathering in of books that go out to the different departments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not ' heard of any complaint of late. I remember some fifteen years ago when the Library Committee had rather a warm discussion over this subject, but at that time no means could be devised by which a check could be put upon this evil practice. We have to trust to the honour of those who took the books away from the library to bring them back again. Many of those books are never returned simply because of carelessness on the part of those who take them out. It was suggested that it would be a good thing to pass a rule that books should not go out-I would not say out of the library, because that would not be possible. but that books should not go out of this building. That. I think, is the only rule that would be satisfactory-that the books in this library like those in any other library of a similar nature should not be taken out of the building. But our library here is really a circulation library
Very much so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Members have the privilege of taking books away, and they also have the privilege of taking them for their friends. This, it seems to me, ought not to be allowed. It is difficult, perhaps, to say that a member of parliament, at the end of the session, for instance, should not be allowed to take books with him. A good many members do that. And I believe that those who use the library most are those who return -books most surely and quickly. But there are members who take away books which happen to strike their fancy and, through sheer eai-elessness, do not return them. Then, members facilitate the taking out of books by then-friends, and this, I believe, is the cause of the disappearance of the larger number of books that are not returned. The redeeming feature of the case is that these books are generally of those that can best be spared from the library. There has hitherto been no great public library in Ottawa, and it has been difficult, when we had a large and valuable collection of books here, to keep that collection closed and not allow any of the books to(go out. But. unless we have a rigid rule to this effect. I am afraid the leakage cannot be stopped.

The right hon. Prime Minister has spoken of this as a circulating library. Well, it has at least one of the elements for circulation. The arteries are there, but whether the veins are there, to complete the circulation by bringing back that which is sent out through the arteries, is a great question. Not only do members get these books, but this library is largely a convenience to the people of Ottawa.

Through the members, or in some way, books are circulated throughout the city. The Prime Minister says that one redeeming feature is that the books thus sent out and often lost are largely of the kind that can best be spared from a library of this kind. But that seems like saying that the people's money is voted each year for the purchase of books which are not useful in assisting members of parliament in their work and are not of the kind for which this library was instituted. X think it would be difficult to make a rule that books shall not be taken from the precincts of this House. One's time as a member is pretty well taken up during the working hours of the House, and unless one can take a book to his room and digest it there, he is denied opportunities which enable him better to carry on his work in this House. But two things might be insisted upon : That the privilege, very much abused by some of us, of handing out..books to all and sundry of our friends, might be curtailed or done away with. And, then, though it might seem a drastic remedy, I think the librarian might be backed up by a rule which would enable him to say to a member that books out must be returned within a reasonable time, otherwise he would not be allowed to take out more books. I am sure that if such a rule were applied in my case it would bring me to time-I would be pretty careful to send books back that I might not be on the prohibited list. But I think the time has come when we should stop this leak. It is impossible to get some books from the library that ought to be there. You ask for them, but they are out. Who has them ? Nobody knows ; they have been out, perhaps, for three or four years. It would surprise some members of the House to see the list of the books that are out, never to come back I suppose, for they have been out so long that they have lost all knowledge of the haunts from which they came. But I think that the suggestions I make if carried out, would result in good.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The next time there is a meeting of the library committee, I will attend if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) will be there, and I will support his suggestions.
I will be there.

I would suggest to the Library Committee an'idea for their consideration at their next meeting. Why not create a fund by asking every member who wishes to take out books put up a cash deposit ; then, if the book is not returned in the proper time, use the money to buy another copy. That is. the way they do in circulating libraries, and it seems to me that that is the proper way to do here.

I would suggest, to the leader of the House that the next Act that is passed adding to the sessional indemnity Mr. FOSTER.
of members should carry a condition that a certain percentage of the increase shall be kept back for one or two years, to be used in supplying the deficiencies caused by books being borrowed and not returned.
Legislation-genera!-.printing, binding and distributing the laws, $7,000.
When will the consolidation of the laws be completed ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is expected that it will be completed this year, and that the Bill will be ready for the next session of xoarliament.
Legislation-general-printing, printing paper and binding, $125,000.
What does that cover '!

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This covers the expenditures of the Printing Bureau on the items stated. There is nothing new in this-it is the usual vote.

I take this opportunity to repeat what I said the other night. The Printing Bureau is a great institution with which, I am sure, many of the members are not familiar. The members of the Printing Committee had occasion to visit the Bureau recently and were astonished to see the work that was done there, especially in the binding of the reports submitted to parliament and the books for the library. The building is not nearly large enough for the work to be done. The King's Printer and his assistanfs all complain of that, and rightly. An addition has been made to the building and is now about ready for occupation, but it will do but little good, for much more room is needed. The government have a large property there, and the sooner they use it the better. There are a great many employees in the Printing Bureau, but, for lack of space they work at a great disadvantage. We are losing money because the place is so small that the employees cannot do their work as well as they would otherwise do if. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) is not here, but, in his absence I' will call the attention of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to this case as one deserving his earnest attention.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron) has mentioned this matter, as it gives me an opportunity to give my hon. friend and to those who take an interest in the subject my own view. I know that the building of the Printing Bureau is altogether too small. The Secretary of State has complained to me more than once and has proposed that provision should be made for increased accommodation. I have stated more than once tc the Secretary of State-and I might just as well make a confession of it now-that the selection of a site for the Printing Bureau was very unfortunate. My opinion is that we should have the whole of that space

vacant, extending Major Hill Park to tlie bank of the river which would add much to the' beauty of Ottawa, but you have the Printing Bureau just where it is, interfering with such a park. It is an ugly building, it has no architectural beauty, and I think if we were to make an addition of one-third or one-half of this building we might very well select another site and leave this site vacant in order to have what we should have, a park which would cover the whole of Nepean Point. I do not know if parliament would entertain that view. The plan would not cost much, it would cost something of course, but it would add very much to the beauty of this city in which we take a good deal of pride, and I think this idea ought to meet with some favour on the part of my hon. friends. At all events this is^an idea which I have not dared to mention very often, but since the matter has come up, I would like gentlemen on the other side to think of the suggestion I have made that if we are to spend a good deal of money in enlarging the Printing Bureau, and we must do it, we might consider the advisability of putting it elsewhere and leaving the space which is now partly vacant absolutely vacant, covering the whole of Nepean Point with a continuation of Major Hill Park.
The new Mint is being built close to that spot which shows that the idea has not been very much thought of.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, the Mint is near Sussex Street. I would have preferred to have it elsewhere, but where it is it will not interfere with the idea I h,ave in my mind of extending Major Hill Park along the river.

Of course that is another question. Whether we are to enlarge the Printing Bureau or place it somewhere else is the Important thing. I believe it would be a saving of money and would improve the good work that is now done there, if the building was enlarged one way or, another.

I dissent entirely from the remarks of the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) with regard to our losing money in this connection. An examination would reveal to any pers'on interested the fact that notwithstanding that the printing of parliament is not entirely done at the Bureau here the country is not suffering as a result, and that being the case I think it will be1 found that the printing done outside the Bureau is done at rates that compare very favourably indeed with the rates paid at the Printing Bureau. I chanced to be present before the Public Accounts Committee when Dr. Dawson gave evidence. He pointed out and satisfied me that in some particular instances he was able to get work done outside
the Bux-eau at rates very much cheaper than he could get the work done at the Bureau. I think upon close examination very many items will be detected in which it will be found that the work can be done more cheaply in printing offices as in connection with' the preparation of the various reports. In some cases this could be done cheaper in Montreal. Toronto, or even some of the smaller cities. This1 is a matter which might very well engage the attention of the Printing Committee, and I desire once again to protest for the present at least, against any further enlargement of the Printing Bureau until it has been shown that the country is saving by it. If the matter is gone into carefully, I think it can. be demonstrated to the satisfaction of parliament that this work can be done by printing concerns throughout the country at rates from which the country not only will not lose, but I have no doubt will gain.

I think I remember the occasion of which my hon. friend speaks. One of the reasons given by the King's Printer was that the building was too small and they could not have all the plant necessary to do all he would like to do. Secondly there was a question of printing the lists, and it was said-and there was a great deal of sense in it-that the printing of Lists for British Columbia or the Northwest Territories for instance, would toe done cheaper as a matter of fact in those provinces than having them printed here, and sent there. Another subject was the printing of maps.
Lithographing.

That kind of work can be done better and cheaper in Toronto or Montreal, because the Printing Bureau here is too small to contain the apparatus necessary. At the same time the King's Printer said he could do everything here, and if my hon. friend will go back a few years to the establishment of the Printing Bureau he will find a great many reasons given in favour of having all the printing of pax-lia-ment done here, not only for reasons of economy but for other reasons. My hon. friend. I am sure, must recognize that there must have been some good reasons given for the establishment of that office here ; indeed. I think it has given satisfaction and the only question I was bring-jug before tlie House was that as the business of the country is enlarging-as we are told and it is true-the printing is enlarging The printing of ' Hansard ' is a great work at the Bureau. The binding is a much gi-eater work at the Bui'eau than I supposed. We have some very good experts in their lines doing that work and when congratulating the King's Printer on such good work we were told that he was handicapped by the small space in which his men were working, and that is the reason why
.6951

I for the second time called the attention of the government to it. I do not think we could vote money for a better purpose. My hon. friend may have the Bureau somewhere else, that is another idela. If parliament decided to put the Bureau somewhere else, if we knew what to do with the old building which is a very costly one, I would have nothing to say, but whether we build-semewhere else or enlarge the present building it is high time to do something. One of the highest officials there suggested that the building could be heightened by a couple of stories which I understand would be tbe cheapest plan. The King's Printer's idea would be to enlarge the building, because there is a good deal of ground there, but of course that is not taking into consideration the plan of my hon. friend. If the building is put somewhere else, all of the demands would probably be met in the new' building.

To my mind the question of public printing being done outside of Ottawa was settled years ago when the present Bureau was established. I confess I have never heard any good reason given since that time .for returning to the old practice of having a portion of the work done in Toronto, Montreal or any other city of the Dominion. I think mvself it is* decidedly better to have the entire work done here under the strict supervision of the government.
Now as to the cost being less when done m some outside office, it is quite possible that the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) may be correct. To my mind, it is absolutely impossible, with the present conveniences for doing the work, to get all the work out of the men that they can do. I had occasion a short time ago to visit the Printing Bureau along with other members ot the Printing Committee. We went through the building, I think through almost all the rooms. I was astonished to see the crowded condition, and because of tbe way that men were huddled together It was absolutely impossible to do work. They had not an opportunity of doing the full amount oi work that a man could do were he given space-not only space to work in, but spact to breathe in. Having spent an hour ami a half in that building. I was glad to gel outside. I fail to see how in the world these people live there. The health conditions are practically .abominable. How those women manage to sit there for eight or ten hours is something 1 could not comprehend, and certainly the sanitary arrangements are far from what they ought to be. We cannot expect to get people to do the amount ol work they should do with such surroundings. " e cannot expect them to perform the same amount of work if they really have not space to breathe in. it only requires a visit for a short time to see that the first requisites of health and of the opportunity Mr. BERGERON.
to do work are absolutely wanting in every department of that building. In regard to the suggestion of the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), certainly something will have to be done, no' matter whether the cost is great or small. The country is losing money and will lose money as long as the present conditions prevail, for the reasons which I have assigned. We want the Printing Bureau to be as near as (possible to the parliament buildings. Many of us have occasion to go there from time to time, and it would be very inconvenient if the Printing Bureau were removed half a mile or a mile from the public buildings here ; in fact, at the present time, even when tbe Printing Bureau is located as it is, I think that very much better conveniences ought to be and could be provided for giving members of parliament access' to the Printing Bureau for the purposes that they require to go there from time to time.
I think the time has come when a foot-way should be so constructed from parliament hill across to the park and to the Printing Bureau so as to give easy access without going around by way of Wellington street and Sussex street, or going through the park, to get there. I have occasion to go at different times when I find that time actually prevents me from doing so. I find it inconvenient, and if we could be assisted in any way by such means as I suggest I know it would inure to tbe benefit and convenience of every member of parliament. Were it not for that I would not object at all in tbe construction of a new building to have it removed to a greater distance, but I fear that by scattering these buildings too much we are going to inconvenience men who have all their time fully occupied in this House if they pretend for a moment to attend to their parliamentary duties. I sympathize with the government in any desire they have to increase the accommodation.
1 confess that at the present time I would favour an enlargement o.f the present building to the suggestion of removing it a considerable distance further away, but certainly it is a matter with which the government will have to deal, and that at a very early date, because the country Is increasing while the conveniences for doing that work are not increasing. I would dislike very much to see a friend of mine go into that Printing Bureau. I think it is destructive to health. I do not know what the exxieri-ence of those who are working there is. but I think ;I made a note of It that I saw depicted on the faces of people who are working there that they are not enjoying the health conditions they ought to enjoy, that they are not able to perform tbe duties which this government and this country would expect them to perform, and that under the present crowded conditions they are not doing what they could do if the conditions were more favourable.

The words of my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) convince me more strongly than ever that the Printing Bureau has undertaken a little more work than it ought to undertake, more particularly under the conditions which he depicts. In spite of what has been said to the com-trary, I still stick to my opinion that this country is not a loser as the result of work being done outside the Printing Bureau, and I am quite satisfied that if my hon. friend had heard the testimony of the King's Printer before the Public Accounts Committee he would share the opinion which I hold, that the fact that work is done outside does not necessarily mean that money is lost to the people of the country. I am quite sure that if the King's Printer finds his work crowded in the Printing Bureau and if he looks around him he can have his work done without entailing any loss to himself or the country. The work would be expedited, and I have no doubt that we could get many returns before we are now able to get them if the King's Printer were to send them to outside offices. The work might necessarily have to go outside the city of Ottawa, but that is no reason why the work should not be done outside. The only condition which should be considered in this connection is that the work should be done at a reasonable price, and the prices that prevail in the printing offices of this country compare very favourably and, in some instances, as I have observed, are lower than the amount for which the work can be done here. I am perfectly well aware, as my hon. friend says, that this is not a new question. This question has probably been decided some years ago, but perhaps, after all, it has not. It is not so absolutely decided that it cannot be resurrected and considered at the present time or in the future, but I do say that it is well worth considering as to whether or not just as good satisfaction can be had by following the suggestion I made in favour of having work done outside as from having it done at the Printing Bureau under the conditions which prevail there. These conditions have been the subject of complaint here. The King's Printer, before the Public Accounts Committee, during the present session, sounded a note of warning. He said that for many years, for as far back, I think, as ten or twelve years, he has been annually bringing this question to the attention of parliament. He prepared a very elaborate report on one occasion pointing out to members of parliament the necessity that existed for the enlargement of the plant there. Of all the members of parliament, there was but one who took any interest in the matter. There was one member out of two hundred and thirteen who took sufficient trouble to read the report which he made to parliament on that occasion, and at the very earliest opportunity that member was defeated. He rather gave it as a warning that nobody should take any further stock 221
in any reports which he put forward as to-the inability of the present plant to cope with the situation. Therefore it is that I throw out the suggestion that before deciding that the plant should be enlarged it would be well to consider whether or not the work could be as well, as cheaply and as expeditiously performed there as elsewhere.
Cantingent expenses in connection with the voters' lists, $40,000.

When this matter was up a few nights ago under the supplementary estimates, I asked the hon Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) how these voters' lists were printed, if they were printed every year and distributed to members. I could tell him, as a matter of fact, that they had not been distributed to me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I tbiuk the lists are printed as fast as they come.
I do not think so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the intention, but as my hon. friend knows, the lists are revised at different times in different provinces. In Quebec and Ontario they are now revised about April, but it often happens that there are appeals.
The final revision takes place before a judge in Ontario.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We do not print the lists until they have the seal of the authority of the final revision. At all events it is the intention of the government to print the lists as fast as they come in.

Does the government print the lists for every constituency each year. Last parliament I know that in some constituencies in New Brunswick they had two lists before I could get one for Lennox, Ontario. I think I only got one voters' list during the whole parliament, and that before the last general election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say how the orders have been carried out, but I understand that the instructions to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery are that as soon as lie receives the lists he shall send them to the Printing Bureau.
Every year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As fast as they come; if they come every year they are sent to the printer.
I think my right hon. friend is mistaken. My recollection is that the lists were only to be printed when an election was to take place.
The law provides that the lists be printed every year.

One of the reasons for repealing tlie old franchise law was because of the expense of printing these lists every year. I am surprised to hear from the right hon. gentleman that the lists are now printed every year. They should only be printed when they are needed. Generally speaking, an election may not be expected for three or four years in most constituencies, and as the lists will be greatly modified before they are needed for our elections, I do not see why they should be printed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think the lists, should not be printed as fast as they come?
I cannot see the use of printing the lists when they are not needed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am glad to hear it, and when next we discuss the matter I will be prepared to give an answer to my hon. friend.

In the province of Ontario, the voters' lists are printed by each municipality every year, and these municipal lists with the same names on them are sent to the Printing Bureau in order to make up the Dominion lists. It seems to me that in any province where each municipality prints the voters' lists every year, it is a useless expenditure to have them reprinted in the Printing Bureau here when the general election comes off. It seems to me that if the government take this matter into their serious consideration, they must arrive at the conclusion that it would be very much better to adopt the lists as they are printed in the province each year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is quite reasonable and for my part I would favour it. I have to say to my hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) that I was wrong in my statement; I am informed that the lists are printed only when they are required.
That is what I understood when the law was passed. How much of this vote did you spend last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say. This is a precaution that is taken in case of an emergency.
This year it may not be needed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It may not. and I do not expect it will.
It might be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It might be ; there is no telling what may take place.
It is not voted with the intention of spending it ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, hut I do not see why we should not gratify even the wildest dreams of gentle nen opposite.

In that event I will not criticise the vote.
Fenian Raid pensions, $2,400.
Will the right hon. gentleman tell us something about the proposed land grant to the Fenian Raid veterans ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That matter is under consideration.

I know cases where the widows of some of the officers who rendered valuable service to the country during the Fenian Raid, have never received pensions in any shape or form. As I understand it the land grant will be given to those who are still living, and it would in no way benefit the widows of deceased veterans. The country appreciates the fact that we owe some debt of gratitude to these people, and the proof is that this vote is always passed without criticism. It seems to me that we should go a little further and that in certain cases where men now deceased have rendered valuable military service to the country in other directions, it would he proper to recognize the services by granting some compensation to the survivors of their families who may be in need of assistance. Would it not be proper for parliament to come to the rescue of these people in the same way that we are now voting these items?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The class of cases to which my hon. friend alludes is of a different character from the class covered here. These pensions on acount of the Jfeuian raid-I speak under correction -must be to persons who were wounded or disabled. My hon. friend .is proposing another class of pensions for military service, out of the ordinary. We? have not under our law given any pensions for that, class of service. Whether we will do it or not is a matter for consideration ; but that is not included in this vote.
Then, I am surprised that the names of'those to whom we pay the pensions are not mentioned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The< names are given, and I will have them for my hon. friend to-morrow.
Compensation to pensioners in lieu of land, $116.76.
This is a small vote, but I think it ought to be explained.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not take the1 trouble to get explanations of these matters, which have been on the votes for several years ; but I will give the explanation to my hon. frietnd on concurrence.

Pensions payable to militiamen on account of the rebellion of 1885, and active services generally, $19,000.

That is the same thing. I belieVe it would be a good thing to have the names. We all know that the United States government is paying more for pensions on account of the Civil War than it did at .the commencement. The pensioners, instead of dying, are increasing in number.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

Then there ought to be a reference in the estimates to the page in the Auditor General's Report.
I understand that there is no extension. These amounts were settled, and if there i.s any change at all, 'it will be a diminution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Exactly. No new name is added. If the name drops, the amount drops accordingly. I will get the names.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not intend to take up this Item this evening, as I do not see present any member from the Northwest, and I would ask that $25,000 for buildings be reserved, and when we take that up, I will give all the explanations I have to give. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: I am afraid it won't do it.

This is taken in case we should have an election in a county. We spent nothing last year on this account, and probably will not spend anything this year ; but we take this money in case there is a vote in a county.

the naturalization papers which are issued in the year.
What other expenses are there ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that there are any others.
How many were naturalized last year ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I could not tell, it is in our records somewhere. I will get it to-morrow.

Is this the secret service fund ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend understands what this is for.
Anything spent last year ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think we spent nearly the whole of it.
Salaries and contingencies of the Paris agency, $6,500.
That requires some explanation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is a very old friend. Mr. Fabre is our commissioner at Paris, and has been since 1881, I believe. Everybody knows the Paris agency, especially those who have been in Paris. The duties performed by Mr. Fabre are well known. He was first appointed commissioner of immigration, but I do not know that he has been very successful in that work. In other respects, however, I think he has been a very efficient and useful officer.	'	i
Outside of immigration, what does he do from year to year ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that he does anything except to keep the office open and furnish information to Canadians. The number of Canadians who now visit Europe is very large. As soon as they reach Paris they go to the commissioner's office for all the information they want, and they get it. They register their names, they have their mail sent there, and are able by means of this agency to keep track of their friends. I think Mr. Fabre renders valuable service in these respects.
What portion of this is for Mr. Fabre's salary ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the greater part is for salary, I could not say how much exactly. But there is the rent of the building to pay, repairs, furniture, &c.
Has he any staff ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He has no staff except a secretary, that he pays out of his own pocket.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, this amount is given to the Royal Academy of Arts in this city. If my memory serves me well, this is a special vote given to a certain society in Ottawa to encourage art-the school of design, I thing.

When is this likely to be brought to an end ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I wish I knew. It has been there to my certain knowledge for ne'arly forty years. It has been gradually decreased every year, but ic has no# yet come to an absolute termination. If my hon. friend asks me when ic will come to an end, I am sorry to say I cannot give him much information, nor, I am afraid, very much hope.
Is no progress being; made ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand there is progress being made1.

It is sometimes hinted that certain gentlemen keep that matter on foot all the time ; it brings in. a certain revenue yearly and it is a matter, of importance to those who are interested to keep it going along. I am not convinced that the difficulties are so great that the matter could not he brought to a termini ation. Surely now, nearly forty years after confederation we should pretty well under^ stand how financial matters rest between the Dominion and the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I really think the government should urge the commissioners to bring in a report covering a final settlement of these old questions. There may be some considerable interest involved, but a hint from the government might do much to bring the matter to an end.

speechtext: I need hardly remind my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) that the mills of the gods grind slow and the mills of the courts grind-

speechtext:
